**The Words He Kept**

My father spent forty years on the radio. Farm reports, school closings, the Saturday swap shop, high school basketball when the regular man had laryngitis. His voice went into strangers' kitchens at six in the morning and told them about rain. People recognized him at the grocery store before they saw him — they'd hear him ask where the vinegar was and turn around. At home he was worse. He was a man who used forty words for vinegar. Dinner took two hours because every meal came with a story, every story had three endings, and he'd back up and take the second one. My mother set a timer once, as a joke. He talked through the buzzer.

He never once ran out of words. That's what I keep coming back to. Sixty-two years, and I never saw him reach for one and come back empty-handed.

The first one he lost was "collar." He called it the neck of the shirt, and we laughed, and he laughed, and it took us a year to understand it wasn't the start of a joke.

Then "avenue." Then the names of birds. Then "perhaps," which he had always used like salt. The neurologist had a word — aphasia — and a phrase — primary progressive — and a metaphor I have never forgiven: the brain is closing rooms. He said it the way a man describes weather.

I started the list at the hospital, on the back of a parking receipt. It began as a joke too: his words, the survivors. It stopped being a joke fast.

At first the losses looked random. They weren't. The fancy words went first, the ones he'd loved showing off — onomatopoeia, peninsula, hullabaloo. Then the abstractions. Justice. Loneliness. Tomorrow lasted longer than I would have guessed.

What stayed was concrete. The needed stuff, the daily bread of language — literally: bread stayed. Water stayed. Out. Keys. Door. The dog's name.

For a while he still talked the way he always had, full speed, no pauses, the old radio cadence — but the sentences had stopped carrying anything. "The morning took it over by the tomorrow," he'd say, comfortable, certain, and look to me for agreement. I agreed. I agreed with everything. That was the winter I learned that fluency is only the sound of language, not the thing itself. He could still say anything. He just couldn't mean it.

Some days he knew. Those were the days he didn't talk at all. He'd sit at the kitchen table with a crossword he could no longer fill in, snapping a pen against his thumb, snap, snap, snap, like a man tapping a wall to find the hollow place.

He tried once to tell me about his own father. Something important — he kept starting over, kept pointing at his chest. After ten minutes he stopped, patted my hand, and said, "Another day." We both knew. We said "another day" to each other for two years after that. It became our word for everything we couldn't say.

My mother had been gone eleven years. Her name — Eleanor — lasted longer than I expected. Longer than mine, at first. He'd see me come through the door and say "Eleanor," and I stopped correcting him sometime in March, because what was I correcting, exactly? Then in the fall I found him at the dresser holding her photograph, and he looked up at me, apologetic, and said, "June."

I'm June.

He never got Eleanor back. My name went everywhere after that. It did everything. It meant her, me, the whole category of women he had loved and trusted.

By the next year he had maybe sixty words. Then thirty. I moved the list from receipts into a notebook, because I finally understood what it was: a tide going out, and me marking the water line.

Here is some of what stayed:

Bread. Water. Door. Out. Wait. Yes. No. Petey. The word for cold. My name.

Petey the dog outlived Eleanor by two years in that mouth. I've made some peace with that. Mostly.

He lost "no" before "yes." I'm still thinking about what that means. Whatever else was being taken, he stayed a man who agreed with the world.

"Out" became a vocabulary of its own. He'd stand at the door in his coat saying it — out, out — and it could mean the yard, the street, the car, anywhere that wasn't this. We walked a lot that year. He pointed at things and I named them, and he'd nod like a farmer reading the sky.

I read to him at the end. He couldn't follow a plot and didn't need one. His face did the listening, leaning toward the sound the way it had always leaned — forty years of his voice going out into the dark, and now one coming back to him. I read him the farm report. Rain developing after midnight. He nodded like a man receiving good news.

The last winter, he had ten words. Nine of them were for asking. Water — and a glass appeared. Out — and there was the door, the coat, the snow, the two of us. Wait — wait. Wait.

The tenth was my name.

He spent it on everything. The blanket, the window, the soup, the light moving along the wall: "June," he'd say, pleased, presenting each thing to me like he'd found it, and in a way he had. I had stopped being a name and become his word for the entire category of good things. It is the most extravagant thing anyone has ever done with my name. Forty years on the radio, a man who never once ran out of words — and at the end, down to one, and the one was mine.

The last morning, it was snowing hard. He was looking past me at the window when he said it, and it wasn't a question and it wasn't a greeting. He said it the way he used to say rain developing after midnight. A man telling you what's coming. What's here. What's true.

"June," he said.

I know, I said. I know.

message.reasoning:
The instruction is simple and open-ended: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you."

This is a creative writing prompt with freedom. The interesting constraint is the word count itself — 1000 words. There's something meta about being given a finite budget of words. I could lean into that: write about the experience of having exactly 1000 words, or use the constraint thematically.

Let me brainstorm directions:

1. **A meditation on the word count itself** — writing about choosing what to do with 1000 words, the economics of language, what's worth saying. Risk: could become navel-gazing and precious.

2. **A short story** — something with actual narrative momentum. A character, a moment, a turn.

3. **An essay on something I find genuinely interesting** — attention, memory, the way language works, something observed.

4. **Hybrid** — begin with the meta-frame and let it dissolve into an actual story or the story emerges from the frame.

The meta approach is tempting but often clichéd ("What should I do with these words...?"). However, if I do it well — if the meditation becomes an actual argument or an actual feeling — it could work. The best version would use the constraint not as a gimmick but as a genuine pressure: what does scarcity do to speech?

Actually, let me think about what "comes to me" honestly. What's alive in my thinking lately?

Ideas that feel genuinely mine:
- The way people talk to each other when they know time is limited (hospital rooms, airports, last days)
- Letters as an art form dying not because of email but because of abundance — when words were expensive (postage, literacy, effort) they were chosen carefully
- The observation that constraint generates style: sonnets, tweets, telegrams, epitaphs
- A story about someone with a literal constraint — a character who can only speak a certain number of words? That's a magical realism premise.
- The epitaph as the ultimate compressed text — a whole life in a line or two

Telegrams! "STOP" — you paid by the word, so families compressed love into fragments. "COMING HOME STOP BRING NOBODY STOP" — the economy of it. That's a rich historical vein.

Or: a story about a dying parent and a child where every word counts. Sentimental risk, but if handled with restraint...

Or something stranger: the premise of a world where everyone is allotted words. Too dystopian-allegorical maybe, and it's been done (like "The Disappearance" or various flash fiction premises).

Let me consider the strongest option. I think a piece that does this:

1. Opens with the immediate honesty of the prompt — I was handed 1000 words, a budget.
2. Uses that as a springboard into the real subject: what scarcity does to language, with concrete textures — telegrams, epitaphs, last words, text messages, the way we speak to the dying.
3. Lands somewhere with actual emotional or intellectual weight — maybe turning personal at the end, or turning toward the reader.

The risk of the essay approach: it could read as a clever performance without a heartbeat. The fix is specificity — real details, real names if I use them carefully, real textures.

Alternatively, a short story with a character. Let me draft a premise: A woman whose father is losing language to aphasia or dementia, and she keeps a notebook of his remaining words. As his vocabulary shrinks, each word gains weight. She learns which words survive longest — "water," "no," her name or maybe not her name, maybe the dog's name, which is its own quiet wound. That's a story about the word budget in reverse: he's spending down to zero and she's watching which words he keeps.

Oh, that's good. That's the inverse of my abundance — he has a shrinking account. The 1000 words I was given mirror the few hundred he has left. That's the resonance.

Let me build that story:

- Narrator: daughter or son. Let's say daughter, or keep it first person ambiguous... first person, a daughter.
- Father: former something wordy? A crossword solver, a teacher, a lawyer, a man who talked for a living — maybe a radio man, a typesetter, a mailman who wrote letters. Actually: a man of many words makes the loss steeper. A trial lawyer? A preacher? A man who told stories at dinner and everyone rolled their eyes and now they'd give anything for one more digression.

- The condition: primary progressive aphasia or a dementia. The words don't leave all at once; they leave like tenants. Concrete details: he reaches for "spoon" and comes back with "the — the for the." He calls the dog "the brother." He keeps nouns he needs: bread, keys. He loses her mother's name before he loses her own? Or the reverse — brutal either way. Maybe: he loses "daughter" as a category but keeps her name. Or loses her name but knows her face, calls her "the girl who comes."

- The notebook: she starts listing his remaining words. The story can move through the list. The list becomes a poem of the ordinary: water, bread, door, dog, wait, yes, no, tomorrow, why.

- The turn: the discovery that grammar goes before words do — he keeps the melody of sentences and fills them with the wrong words, so he still "talks" fluently but meaning drains out. That's actually how some aphasias work (fluent/Wernicke's). Or the reverse: he knows exactly what he wants and can't find the door to it.

- Emotional spine: what's the last word? What word does she want him to keep? Maybe "wait." Maybe her name. Maybe "yes."

- Ending: not sentimental resolution, but one clean image. Perhaps: near the end he has maybe ten words, and one of them is her name, and he uses it not as her name but as a word for everything good — "Mary" for the window, for the soup, for the light. Her name becomes his word for "love" or "yes" or "good." That's the ending. That's the emotional payoff: she's the last noun standing, and he spends her name on everything.

That's genuinely moving if I write it with restraint. No melodrama. Short declaratives. Let the details do the work.

Structure sketch (~1000 words, so I need to budget too — fitting, and I shouldn't point at that too hard; maybe one light touch at the start or none at all. Actually the prompt gave me 1000 words; I could acknowledge it in a single opening line and then vanish into the story, or not acknowledge it at all. I think a very brief bridge is honest and elegant: one or two sentences acknowledging the gift/constraint, then the story. Or skip it entirely. Let me try skipping it — a clean title and the story. Hmm. The user said "write whatever comes to you" — pure freedom. I think starting directly with the story is stronger. Maybe a title.)

Title ideas: "The Last Noun." "His Remaining Words." "Word List." "The Inventory." "Remaining." I like "The Last Noun" — it telegraphs a bit but intriguingly. Or "The Words He Kept." Let me go with something quiet: "The Words He Kept" is nice and plain.

Draft the story:

Opening: establish the father as a man of surplus language. He was a man who used ten words where one would do — the family joke. He read the dictionary? He did crosswords in ink. He narrated the weather like a verdict. At dinner he told stories with three false endings. Give him a profession: high school English teacher? Trial lawyer? Radio announcer — "He spent thirty years reading the farm report and school closings on AM radio" — that's specific and warm and regional. Good. His voice was in strangers' kitchens. People recognized him at the grocery store by his voice, not his face. Lovely detail.

Then the diagnosis: not dramatic. The first loss was small — he couldn't find "collar," called it "the neck of the shirt," which everyone found funny, even him. Then more substitutions. The neurologist's word: aphasia, primary progressive. A disease that spends language down to nothing. "The brain, the doctor said, was closing rooms."

The notebook: she starts the list almost as a joke, then as vigil. The list is the spine of the story — I can render it in fragments. First the rare words go: "onomatopoeia," "peninsula," the names of birds (he was a birder? maybe too much — keep it lean). Adjectives thin out. Abstractions go early: "justice," "lonely," "perhaps." What stays: concrete, needed, beloved words. Water. Bread. Out. Dog's name. Door. Again. Wait.

Middle beats:
- The grammar point: for a while he still spoke in full sentences, fluent and confident, but the meaning emptied — sentences like "The morning put it over there by the tomorrow." Or the reverse, halting. Choose one: I'll use the fluent-empty phase briefly, it's eerie and true.
- A scene: he tries to tell her something important — a story about his own father? — and she watches him circle the landing field of the sentence, unable to touch down. He gets angry, or he laughs, or he pats her hand and says, "Another day." Which is a lie they both accept. "Another day" — good, and it becomes recurring.
- Her mother — is the mother alive? Simpler if it's just the two of them, mother gone years ago. Then the wound: he keeps calling her by the mother's name. Then he loses the mother's name too, and one day uses the narrator's name for the mother's photograph. Names migrating.
- The name migration is the engine of the ending. So: mother's name appears mid-story, he uses narrator's name on the photo of the mother — meaning: the women he loved collapsed into one word, hers.

Ending: the word count gets down to almost nothing. Ten words? She reads to him now instead. He likes being read to — his face does the listening. Last words inventory, final: her name. And he uses her name for everything: the blanket, the window, the soup, the light on the wall, her. She stops correcting anything. The name means yes or good or please or love. Final line options: something like — "By the end it was the only word he had left, and he spent it on everything, and it was enough." Or: he says her name to the snow coming down outside. Or the very last exchange: she says "I'm here" and he answers with her name — which is his yes.

Let me also give her a name. Something plain and era-appropriate: Ruth? Alice? June? Let's say "June." Nice — the month, warm, one syllable, sounds like a word a mouth would keep. Father's name: Walter? Frank? "Herbert"? Let's say "Walt" — short, and a radio-adjacent name. Or no name for the narrator beyond June.

Radio detail: he said "W-A-L-T" as station call letters? Cute, maybe too cute. Could do: he'd sign off, "This is Walter Kowalski, signing off" — no, keep the surname simple: "Walter Doyle." Fine, or leave surname out.

Now, word budget. ~1000 words. Let me allocate:
- Opening, the man of surplus words + radio: ~180 words
- The losses begin, doctor, closing rooms: ~150
- The notebook begins, early list: ~150
- Middle scenes: fluent emptiness, "Another day," name migration: ~250
- Decline, reading to him, final list: ~150
- Ending, her name as his last word, spent on everything: ~120

Total ~1000. I'll aim for the actual story to land near 1000; I don't need to hit exactly, but close is respectful of the frame. Let me write it with care.

Style notes: plain sentences, concrete nouns, minimal adverbs, no crying on the page. The emotion lives in the details. Avoid medical jargon beyond one use of "aphasia." Avoid explaining the metaphor of the word budget explicitly — let the reader feel it. Maybe one faint echo: "He was a man who had never once in his life run out of words" early, and the arc closes that.

One more consideration: should I frame it with any note to the user? The user said "write whatever comes to you." I think the cleanest response is the piece itself, maybe with a title. No preamble needed, or a single-line preamble at most. I'll go with just the title and the story. Format: prose, no headers beyond a title. Paragraph breaks. A few one-line paragraphs for the word lists to give them visual weight. Italics maybe not needed; plain text lists.

He never once ran out of words. That's what I keep coming back to. Sixty-two years, and I never saw him reach for one and come back empty-handed.

The first one he lost was "collar." He called it the neck of the shirt, and we laughed, and he laughed, and it took us a year to understand it wasn't the start of a joke.

Then "avenue." Then the names of birds. Then "perhaps," which he had always used like salt. The neurologist had a word — aphasia — and a phrase — primary progressive — and a metaphor I have never forgiven: the brain is closing rooms. He said it the way a man describes weather.

I started the list at the hospital, on the back of a parking receipt. It began as a joke too: his words, the survivors. It stopped being a joke fast.

At first the losses looked random. They weren't. The fancy words went first, the ones he'd loved showing off — onomatopoeia, peninsula, hullabaloo. Then the abstractions. Justice. Loneliness. Tomorrow lasted longer than I would have guessed.

What stayed was concrete. The needed stuff, the daily bread of language — literally: bread stayed. Water stayed. Out. Keys. Door. The dog's name.

For a while he still talked the way he always had, full speed, no pauses, the old radio cadence — but the sentences had stopped carrying anything. "The morning took it over by the tomorrow," he'd say, comfortable, certain, and look to me for agreement. I agreed. I agreed with everything. That was the winter I learned that fluency is only the sound of language, not the thing itself. He could still say anything. He just couldn't mean it.

Some days he knew. Those were the days he didn't talk at all. He'd sit at the kitchen table with a crossword he could no longer fill in, snapping a pen against his thumb, snap, snap, snap, like a man tapping a wall to find the hollow place.

He tried once to tell me about his own father. Something important — he kept starting over, kept pointing at his chest. After ten minutes he stopped, patted my hand, and said, "Another day." We both knew. We said "another day" to each other for two years after that. It became our word for everything we couldn't say.

My mother had been gone eleven years. Her name — Eleanor — lasted longer than I expected. Longer than mine, at first. He'd see me come through the door and say "Eleanor," and I stopped correcting him sometime in March, because what was I correcting, exactly? Then in the fall I found him at the dresser holding her photograph, and he looked up at me, apologetic, and said, "June."

I'm June.

He never got Eleanor back. My name went everywhere after that. It did everything. It meant her, me, the whole category of women he had loved and trusted.

By the next year he had maybe sixty words. Then thirty. I moved the list from receipts into a notebook, because I finally understood what it was: a tide going out, and me marking the water line.

Here is some of what stayed:

Bread. Water. Door. Out. Wait. Yes. No. Petey. The word for cold. My name.

Petey the dog outlived Eleanor by two years in that mouth. I've made some peace with that. Mostly.

He lost "no" before "yes." I'm still thinking about what that means. Whatever else was being taken, he stayed a man who agreed with the world.

"Out" became a whole vocabulary of its own. He'd stand at the door in his coat saying it — out, out — and it could mean the yard, the street, the car, anywhere that wasn't this. We walked a lot that year. He pointed at things and I named them, and he'd nod like a farmer reading the sky.

I read to him at the end. He couldn't follow a plot and didn't need one. His face did the listening, leaning toward the sound the way it had always leaned — forty years of his voice going out into the dark, and now one coming back to him. I read him the farm report. Rain developing after midnight. He nodded like a man receiving good news.

The last winter, he had ten words. Nine of them were for asking. Water — and a glass appeared. Out — and there was the door, the coat, the snow, the two of us. Wait — wait. Wait.

The tenth was my name.

He spent it on everything. The blanket, the window, the soup, the light moving along the wall: "June," he'd say, pleased, presenting each thing to me like he'd found it, and in a way he had. I had stopped being a name and become his word for the entire category of good things. It is the most extravagant thing anyone has ever done with my name. Forty years on the radio, a man who never once ran out of words — and at the end, down to one, and the one was mine.

The last morning, it was snowing hard. He was looking past me at the window when he said it, and it wasn't a question and it wasn't a greeting. He said it the way he used to say rain developing after midnight. A man telling you what's coming. What's here. What's true.

"June," he said.

I know, I said. I know.

Petey the dog outlived Eleanor by two years in that mouth. I've made some peace with that. Mostly.

He lost "no" before "yes." I'm still thinking about what that means. Whatever else was being taken, he stayed a man who agreed with the world.

"Out" became a whole vocabulary of its own. He'd stand at the door in his coat saying it — out, out — and it could mean the yard, the street, the car, anywhere that wasn't this. We walked a lot that year. He pointed at things and I named them, and he'd nod like a farmer reading the sky.

I read to him at the end. He couldn't follow a plot and didn't need one. His face did the listening, leaning toward the sound the way it had always leaned — forty years of his voice going out into the dark, and now one coming back to him. I read him the farm report. Rain developing after midnight. He nodded like a man receiving good news.

The last winter, he had ten words. Nine of them were for asking. Water — and a glass appeared. Out — and there was the door, the coat, the snow, the two of us. Wait — wait. Wait.

The tenth was my name.

He spent it on everything. The blanket, the window, the soup, the light moving along the wall: "June," he'd say, pleased, presenting each thing to me like he'd found it, and in a way he had. I had stopped being a name and become his word for the entire category of good things. It is the most extravagant thing anyone has ever done with my name. Forty years on the radio, a man who never once ran out of words — and at the end, down to one, and the one was mine.

The last morning, it was snowing hard. He was looking past me at the window when he said it, and it wasn't a question and it wasn't a greeting. He said it the way he used to say rain developing after midnight. A man telling you what's coming. What's here. What's true.

"June," he said.

I know, I said. I know.
